newsitem.title: POLAND: Battle over abortion continues after Polish vote.
newsitem.headline: Battle over abortion continues after Polish vote.

text.p: A bitter debate raged on in Poland after parliament passed a long-contested bill liberalising the country's tough anti-abortion law.

Opponents of the bill, grouped around pro-Catholic rightist parties and the Solidarity trade union, vowed to challenge it in the Constitutional Tribunal which checks whether new laws conform with the constitution.
Solidarity said it would also campaign on the issue in next year's parliamentary polls and reverse the bill if it won.

"Only enemies of our nation could vote for liberalisation," Marian Pilka, head of the rightist Christian National Alliance (ZChN), told PAP news agency after parliament voted by 228 to 195 on Thursday to relax the current legislation.
The Catholic Church said it would try to dissuade women from resorting to abortion, which it views as killing, partly by gathering financial support for those in hardship.
Some of the bill's supporters said they feared new liberal regulations could be hard to implement in the present climate because of pressure on doctors, teachers and others.

"I am convinced that women who want legal abortions under the new law may have problems, especially in small towns, as the pressure on doctors is so strong," said Wanda Nowicka, director of the Federation for Women and Family Planning.

Under the outgoing law, passed in 1993 by a pro-Catholic government, abortion is allowed only if pregnancy threatens a woman's life or health, results from the crimes of incest or rape, or when the foetus is hopelessly damaged.
Women will now be able to end pregnancies before the 12th week if they face financial or personal problems, but only after qualified counselling and three days of reflection.
The bill extends the 12-week time limit for abortions in rape and incest cases, which Nowicka said might be a problem given the slow workings of the justice system.
The bill provides for sex education classes in schools from September next year and cheaper contraception -- steps designed to reduce unintentional pregnancies leading to abortions.
As before, penalties for breaking the abortion law -- ranging up to eight years in jail -- will fall on doctors and others abetting abortions, not on women undergoing them.
Abortions will be available for free in state clinics, while private establishments will be tightly regulated, unlike the underground clinics now operating for those with money.
Nowicka welcomed the bill's passage, saying that after the existing law took effect in 1993, reports of abandoned babies or infanticide doubled from about 200 a year to 500.
She rejected arguments that it would mark a return to the pre-1993 communist-era law of 1956, which led to widespread abortion as there was poor sex education and contraception.
But she told Reuters the new sex education provisions, questioned by the Church, would be hard to implement at first because of a lack of suitable teachers and secular textbooks.
Poland's Supreme Medical Council, to which all doctors belong, opposed the new bill, saying it was unethical to conduct abortions if both mother and foetus were healthy.

The head of the Council's ethics committee, Jerzy Umiastowski, told PAP: "Poland will pay a price in deteriorating health of women, moral confusion, a lowering of doctors' prestige and in demographic catastrophe."
